differences.title: 1. PRIMARY STORAGE MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Apache Druid stores data in immutable, time-partitioned segments with pre-aggregated rollup support. Queries hit segment indexes and aggregators directly, minimizing row scans through columnar-like layouts specialized for OLAP workloads.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse persists data in columnar blocks inside data parts, typically partitioned by date or key ranges. It uses vectorized execution and late materialization, reading only required columns and applying filters/aggregations efficiently per part.

differences.title: 2. INGESTION PATH
differences.leftDesc: Druid ingestion uses configurable indexing tasks (e.g., Kafka indexing) that write immutable segments and can build rollups as data lands. It decouples ingestion from query serving via segment publishing and hot-swappable availability.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse commonly ingests via tables with continuous inserts, including Kafka engines and materialized views for streaming-to-OLAP. Data is continuously appended then merged in the background into larger parts, keeping ingestion fast.

differences.title: 3. QUERY EXECUTION STRATEGY
differences.leftDesc: Druid’s query layer (broker/brokered execution) fans out to historical and real-time nodes, then merges results. It leverages segment-level indexing (e.g., time, dimensions) to prune work before aggregation.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse builds query pipelines executed in parallel across threads/nodes, pushing filters and projections early. It performs aggregation using hash or streaming strategies, often with specialized sorting/order by to accelerate group-by.

differences.title: 4. INDEXING & PRUNING MECHANISMS
differences.leftDesc: Druid maintains segment-level metadata and specialized indexes for time and dimensions, enabling aggressive pruning of segments and blocks. Rollups reduce the number of rows needing aggregation by storing aggregated states per time bucket.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse uses primary key and partitioning for data skipping indexes, plus optional secondary indexes (e.g., min-max, set, bloom filters). It can skip entire data parts or ranges, reducing I/O and speeding query execution.

differences.title: 5. DISTINCT / HIGH-CARDINALITY TOOLS
differences.leftDesc: Druid supports approximation-first patterns like theta sketches and other sketch-based aggregations for distinct counts, integrated into rollups and query-time aggregation. This keeps memory predictable for high-cardinality analytics over time slices.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse provides both exact distinct (e.g., using GROUP BY) and approximate variants like uniq sketches (e.g., HyperLogLog-like). It can trade accuracy for memory/CPU and uses streaming aggregation to handle large groups.

differences.title: 6. CONCURRENCY & UPDATE MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Druid emphasizes immutability: new data publishes new segments, while older segments remain queryable. Updates are typically handled by re-ingesting data or using replace semantics upstream rather than in-place row mutation.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse follows MergeTree family mechanics: inserts append; background merges reorganize parts. It supports limited updates via ALTER/UPDATE with mutations (as new parts are produced), but heavy random updates can be costly versus append-only design.

differences.title: 7. DISTRIBUTED TOPOLOGY & SCALING
differences.leftDesc: Druid scaling is commonly split into historical (queryable immutable segments) and real-time (serving the latest ingested data with special storage). Brokers coordinate requests; coordination policies help balance latency and freshness.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse distributes by sharding datasets across nodes with replication for fault tolerance. Distributed tables route queries to shards, where local parallel execution runs before results are merged centrally or hierarchically.
